items.item: SPJ's own SQL configs (`spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.pushPartValues.enabled`, `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.allowJoinKeysSubsetOfPartitionKeys.enabled`, `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.allowCompatibleTransforms.enabled`) extend shuffle elimination to cases classic bucketing never covers at all: a missing partition value on one side, a join that uses only some of the partition columns, or partition transforms that are compatible but not byte-identical — each a separate, narrower optimisation this topic names but does not independently measure.

at.out: SPJ's own extension configs named only; this topic measures classic Hive bucketing and names SPJ's basic mechanism, not its own further optimisations

items.item: `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.partiallyClusteredDistribution.enabled` handles skew specifically inside SPJ by choosing one side as the big table and partially clustering its splits while replicating the other side's matching splits — a distinct, later-stage mechanism from the plain requirement-based elimination this topic measures with classic bucketing.

at.out: SPJ's own skew-handling config named only, as a separate mechanism from this topic's own measured elimination

items.item: Bucketing and SPJ both exercise the identical planner mechanism as this chapter's own exchange-elimination topic (hash/range partitioning): Catalyst's `EnsureRequirements` rule checking whether an existing output partitioning already satisfies a required distribution — bucketing and SPJ differ only in HOW the existing partitioning got there (an explicit `bucketBy` call vs. a DSv2 catalog's own reported partitioning), not in the planner rule that then exploits it.

at.out: the shared EnsureRequirements mechanism named only, connecting this topic to the earlier exchange-elimination topic rather than re-measuring it

items.item: A stale bucketing pitfall this topic's own examples.py doesn't reproduce directly: appending new rows to an already-bucketed table with a writer that ignores the table's own bucket spec (or via a non-Spark tool) can silently violate the bucketing invariant per-file, after which Spark's own bucketed read still claims the optimisation but returns wrong join results rather than merely losing the speedup — a correctness hazard, not just a performance one.

at.out: the correctness-hazard version of stale bucketing (a writer violating the invariant silently) named only; this topic's own measurement covers the simpler, safe case of an honestly-different bucket count that Spark itself detects and falls back from

items.item: Partitioning a table by a column (`partitionBy`, directory-based) and bucketing it by a different column (`bucketBy`) can be combined on the same table — the two mechanisms are independent and stack, one producing Hive-style directories, the other a fixed hash split inside each directory, as shown directly in Spark's own Generic Load/Save Functions example (`users_partitioned_bucketed`).

at.out: combining partitionBy and bucketBy on the same table named only, from the source's own example; this topic's own examples.py measures bucketing alone

items.item: Sorting within each bucket (`sortBy`, used in both this topic's own examples.py calls) is a separate, optional refinement on top of bucketing itself: it lets a later sort-merge join skip the per-partition sort step too, not just the shuffle, when the sort order also matches — a further elimination this topic's own plan-text assertions do not separately isolate from the Exchange-count measurement.

at.out: sort-merge-join's own further sort-skipping benefit from matching sortBy named only; this topic's own assertions measure the Exchange count, not whether the Sort node itself was also eliminated

items.item: `spark.sql.requireAllClusterKeysForCoPartition` (default true) requires the join's clustering keys to match the partition keys exactly, in the same order, for SPJ's co-partitioning to apply at all — a stricter default than classic bucketing's own matching rule, which this topic's own examples.py keeps at its default throughout.

at.out: SPJ's own stricter default clustering-key-order requirement named only; this topic's own examples.py runs with every config at its default

items.item: Bucket pruning (this chapter's own next-but-one topic territory, adjacent to static partition pruning covered two topics back) skips whole bucket files by a hash of the filter value rather than a directory name — a related but distinct pruning granularity from both this topic's own join-shuffle-elimination measurement and the earlier topic's own directory-level static pruning.

at.out: bucket pruning named only as a related, finer-grained mechanism distinct from this topic's own join-elimination measurement

items.item: A bucketed table's bucket count is fixed at write time and cannot be changed without rewriting the entire table — unlike `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, a session-level knob a later query can simply set differently, bucketing's own commitment is a physical, on-disk one that every future reader and writer of that table must agree with indefinitely.

at.out: the permanence of a bucket count as a physical commitment, contrasted with the earlier topic's own session-level shuffle-partition knob, named only

items.item: Iceberg's own `bucket(N, col)` partition transform (shown directly in the Performance Tuning docs' own SPJ example) is itself one specific partition-transform function among several a DSv2 catalog can register (others include identity, truncate and the time-based transforms), making Hive-style `bucketBy` a special case of a much larger transform vocabulary SPJ's own mechanism was built to generalise over.

at.out: Iceberg's own broader transform-function vocabulary beyond bucket() named only, from the source's own example
